summary: Describes the Telnet server interface on IBM's iSeries midrange computers, which lets clients request terminal or printer sessions with specific attributes such as device names, encryption, language support and auto-sign-on. This memo is informational.

eli5.summary: Old business computers from IBM had a special way to log in over Telnet. This note writes down the extra requests a client may make, such as choosing which screen or printer name to use.

questions: how does iseries telnet auto sign on
subtitle: How a Telnet client asks an IBM iSeries server for a particular terminal or printer session, and signs on automatically.

tldr.problem: A plain Telnet client could not choose device names, language settings or printers on an IBM iSeries server, or sign on without the sign-on panel.
tldr.mechanism: The client sends custom USERVAR variables through the Telnet Environment option (RFC 1572), including device name, keyboard type, auto-sign-on credentials (plain text, DES or SHA substitutes, or a Kerberos ticket) and printer attributes, and the server can answer with a Startup Response Record.
tldr.outcome: The memo is Informational, replaces RFC 2877, and carries an IESG note that it is not a candidate for any level of Internet Standard.

today: RFC 4777 is an Informational memo that replaces RFC 2877, adding sections for Kerberos, SHA-1, security and IANA considerations. It is not a candidate for any level of Internet Standard, and the unit metadata shows no later RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: What the iSeries Telnet Server Offers
sections.content:
The iSeries Telnet server lets clients negotiate both terminal and printer device names through Telnet Environment option negotiation (RFC 1572). A client can ask for a pre-defined device by name. If none exists, the device is created, and the client can negotiate attributes such as the code page, character set and keyboard type.

Printers are requested with new terminal types, and the server can accept a user profile and password so the client bypasses the sign-on panel. For that bypass to succeed, the server setting QRMTSIGN must be *VERIFY or *SAMEPRF.

An IESG note says the IETF disclaims any knowledge of the fitness of this RFC for any purpose, and that publication was not based on IETF review of security, congestion control or interaction with deployed protocols.
sections.eli5: It lets your computer tell an old IBM server which screen or printer you want, and who you are, before the server even asks.

sections.title: Option Negotiation Sequence
sections.content:
Normal Telnet negotiation starts when the server invites the client to negotiate terminal type, then the options needed for 5250 or 3270 block mode: EOR, BINARY and SGA. The server then creates the virtual device. In the enhanced flow, the server bundles an invitation to use NEW-ENVIRON with the terminal type invitation. The client either refuses with WONT NEW-ENVIRON or sends its environment variables, up to a maximum of 1024 bytes of environment strings.

Timing matters. The server creates the device at the first opportunity it thinks it has all the attributes. For a 5250 device that is the moment TERMINAL-TYPE, BINARY and EOR are negotiated, so later NEW-ENVIRON data has no effect. The RFC advises clients to send NEW-ENVIRON data as soon as possible, preferably before TERMINAL-TYPE.

Environment option defines six standard VARs: USER, JOB, ACCT, PRINTER, SYSTEMTYPE and DISPLAY. The server uses only USER, as the user profile for auto-sign-on; the others are passed to an initialization exit program.
sections.eli5: The client has to hand over its wish list quickly. Once the server has the basics, it builds the device, and anything the client says later is too late.

sections.title: Display Devices and Name Collisions
sections.content:
New USERVARs let a client create or select a virtual display device. DEVNAME is the device name, KBDTYPE the keyboard type, CODEPAGE and CHARSET the language settings, IBMSENDCONFREC asks for a Startup Response Record, and IBMASSOCPRT names a printer to associate with the display. Device names are up to 10 characters. CODEPAGE and CHARSET must be paired with KBDTYPE, or they default to system values. System object names must be English uppercase, so clients should send uppercase ASCII, which the server converts to EBCDIC.

If the requested name is already in use, the server sends SEND USERVAR "DEVNAME" to ask for another. The client replies with a new name. The server keeps asking until it gets an unused name or the same name twice in a row, in which case it disconnects the client.
sections.eli5: If the seat you asked for is taken, the server asks you to pick another. If you keep naming the same taken seat, it sends you home.

sections.title: Auto-Sign-On and Password Protection
sections.content:
Three sign-on styles are supported: plain text password, an encrypted password substitute, and a Kerberos ticket. For encryption, the server sends a random seed in a USERVAR named IBMRSEED followed by an 8-byte hex value. The client makes its own 8-byte seed and returns it in IBMRSEED with the encrypted password in IBMSUBSPW. Section 5.1 describes a 7-step DES-based substitute and section 5.2 a SHA-1 based one, with worked examples.

For plain text, the client seed is left empty (preferred) or set to hexadecimal zeros. If the password is invalid or expired, the sign-on panel is not bypassed. Binary values must be escaped or byte stuffed as RFC 854 requires, so bytes that look like IAC, VAR, VALUE, ESC or USERVAR are not misread.

For Kerberos, IBMTICKET carries the complete GSS token, up to 16384 bytes, obtained from a Key Distribution Center. Extra USERVARs IBMCURLIB, IBMIMENU and IBMPROGRAM set the current library, initial menu and program to call.
sections.eli5: Instead of shouting your password, you scramble it with a secret number the server gave you plus one of your own. Only the real server can unscramble it.

sections.title: Printers and the Startup Response Record
sections.content:
Printer sessions use the same DEVNAME USERVAR plus printer-specific ones such as IBMMSGQNAME, IBMFONT, IBMFORMFEED, IBMTRANSFORM and IBMMFRTYPMDL. Paper source and envelope values are one-byte hex fields that map to names like *LETTER, *A4 and *NONE through a table in the RFC. The two new printer terminal types are IBM-5553-B01 (double-byte) and IBM-3812-1 (single-byte). Pass-through mode needs at least Transmit-Binary, End-Of-Record and Terminal-Type.

When negotiation finishes, the server powers on the virtual device and, if asked, sends a Startup Response Record with a response code, the system name and the device name. The RFC's examples show code I902 for success and 8902 for a device that is not available. Later sections describe print records, print complete records and null print records for the steady-state pass-through interface.
sections.eli5: After you ask for a printer, the server sends back a short receipt that says whether it worked and which printer you got.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Encrypted passwords protect only the login password, not the whole Telnet session. Encrypting the session requires another protocol layer, such as SSL. Plain text passwords are supported but strongly discouraged, and administrators may configure their systems to reject them. The RFC also notes that plain text exchange cannot be guaranteed safe unless the network is physically protected or trusted, and that networks open to IP address spoofing or directly connected to the Internet should use encrypted exchange.

The IANA section says IBM-3812-1 and IBM-5553-B01 were registered as terminal types.
sections.eli5: Scrambling the password hides your key, but everything else you type can still be read, so use plain text passwords only on networks you trust.

messages.label: IS DEVNAME MYDEVICE1 ...
messages.note: Server tries to select MYDEVICE1, which is in use.

messages.label: SEND DEVNAME
messages.note: Server asks for a single variable.

messages.label: IS DEVNAME MYDEVICE2
messages.note: A new name; if it is the same as before, the server disconnects.
